title: The morning offering
hook: offering the whole day, its work and joys and troubles
tomorrow: why did a hungry man climb onto a roof at midday?

segments.voice: Yesterday, waking: the first word of the day goes to God, before the screen. First thought, God. Today, what that first word can hand over.
screen: `FIRST THOUGHT, GOD.` → `WHAT DOES IT HAND OVER?`

segments.voice: A day arrives like a package with no packing slip. A test, an email, maybe a laugh, maybe bad news, none of it opened yet. Some Christians give the whole box away before it's opened. They call it a morning offering: the day's work, joys and troubles, handed to God at the start. And Christians disagree, kindly, about how it should be said.
screen: `A PACKAGE WITH NO PACKING SLIP.` → `GIVEN AWAY UNOPENED.` → `BUT HOW SHOULD IT BE SAID?`

segments.voice: The idea comes from Paul, writing to the Romans: “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” Bodies: the whole person who'll walk through the day. A sacrifice that stays alive and goes to work. Now the two views. One side says: use words the church has prayed before you. Catholics have a prayer called the Morning Offering, which offers to Jesus the day's prayers, works, joys and sufferings. Thomas Ken, an English bishop, wrote a morning hymn asking God to direct all he plans, does or says that day. Their best case: Jesus gave his followers set words himself, “After this manner therefore pray ye,” and the Psalms are a book of set prayers. Set words carry you on mornings when your own have gone. The other side says: speak plainly, in your own words. Their best case comes from the same chapter of Matthew, a few lines earlier: “use not vain repetitions.” Words you mean, they say, over words you recite. One to tell a friend: both sides quote Jesus in Matthew six. And both agree on what goes in: all of it. A psalm says, “My times are in thy hand.” Times, plural, the good hour and the hard one. Some Christians keep both: a set line on rushed mornings, their own words on slow ones.
screen: `A LIVING SACRIFICE.` · `SET WORDS: AFTER THIS MANNER PRAY.` · `OWN WORDS: NO VAIN REPETITIONS.` · `MY TIMES ARE IN THY HAND.` · then, large: `ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Say out loud, at speaking volume, three things today holds: one task, one thing you're looking forward to, one thing you dread. If you pray, hand all three over, in set words you know or in your own; if not, simply let none of the three be left off the list.
The morning offering. Handing the whole day to God at its start: its work, its joys and its troubles.
Your line: all of it. Set words or your own, the offering leaves nothing out. Day 1683, offered.

screen: `DAY 1683 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 2 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DID A HUNGRY MAN CLIMB ONTO A ROOF AT MIDDAY?`

howItsDone: Some Catholics pray the Morning Offering on waking; other Christians offer the day to God in a morning hymn, a set prayer or their own words.

chat.says: Pop reads the same offering card every morning. i just talk to God. whose way is more legit?
options: Neither. Both sides quote Matthew 6 and offer all of it. Ask him why the card.
His. Set prayers are the official ones, so they count for more.
Yours. Saying the same words daily is what Jesus warned against.
chat.meaning: Christians argue it both ways from the same chapter of Matthew. What both ways offer is the same: the whole day, all of it.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: debate; Grace: Pop reads the same printed morning offering every day; Grace prays in her own words; a kind disagreement at breakfast).

Debate shape: set words (the Morning Offering, Ken's hymn; Matthew 6:9; the Psalms as prayers) versus one's own words (Matthew 6:7). Both cases are stated at their best and neither is ranked. Confirm that the 'own words' view is fairly described for free-church Protestants and that the 'set words' view is fair to Catholic, Orthodox and liturgical Protestant readers.
Matthew 6:7 is quoted only as 'use not vain repetitions' (the full verse continues 'as the heathen do'); confirm the cut is fair.
The Morning Offering is described, not quoted; its wording varies by version. Ken's stanza is paraphrased.
The practice invites the listener to hand the day over 'in set words you know or in your own'; it writes no prayer.
